extraction.name: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100
extraction.description: Two labeled subsets of the tiny images dataset created to provide reliable class labels. The CIFAR-10 set has 6000 examples of each of 10 classes and the CIFAR-100 set has 600 examples of each of 100 non-overlapping classes. Images are 32x32 colour images derived from the tiny images dataset.
extraction.creator: Alex Krizhevsky
extraction.citeAs: Krizhevsky, Alex. Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images. April 8, 2009.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The labeled subsets were collected by paying students to label a subset of the tiny images dataset. Since each image already came with a noisy label from the search term used to find it, labelers filtered out mislabeled images. Each labeler was given a class and asked to examine all images found with that class as the search term, as well as images found with search terms that are WordNet hyponyms of the main search term. Labelers rejected images that did not belong to their assigned class. Every submitted label was personally verified by the author. Duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm using a liberal rejection threshold to capture perfect duplicates and re-saved JPEGs. The dataset was then divided into training and test sets, with 5000 randomly selected training images from each CIFAR-10 class. The CIFAR-100 dataset was collected with identical methodology.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data source was the tiny images dataset collected by colleagues at MIT and NYU over six months by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in WordNet using several search engines including Google, Flickr, and AltaVista, keeping roughly the first 3000 results for each search term. The dataset contains 80 million colour images downscaled to 32x32 and spread across 79,000 search terms.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The tiny images dataset was collected over the span of six months; the paper is dated April 8, 2009. No explicit start and end dates are given for the CIFAR labeling.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Images were downscaled to 32x32. Perfect duplicates and images with an excessively large portion of white pixels were removed from the tiny images dataset. For the labeled subsets, duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm using a threshold liberal enough to capture perfect duplicates and re-saved JPEGs. The CIFAR-10 dataset was split into training and test sets, with 5000 randomly selected training images from each class.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For experiments, data preprocessing included ZCA whitening to decorrelate pixels and set variance in each dimension to 1. In later experiments, the 1000 least significant principal components were deleted by setting corresponding entries of the diagonal matrix to zero. Some experiments used whitened data and others used unwhitened data with the 1000 least-significant directions of variance removed.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Students were paid to label images by filtering mislabeled examples from the tiny images dataset. Labelers were assigned a class and examined images retrieved with that class term and its WordNet hyponyms. They were instructed to include an image if the class name would be high on the list of likely answers to 'What is in this picture?', to reject line drawings and cartoons, to require only one prominent instance of the object, and to allow unusual viewpoints or partial occlusion if identity was still clear. They were told false positives were worse than false negatives. Every submitted label was personally verified by the author. CIFAR-100 used identical methodology.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The dataset already came with noisy labels from web search terms, and human labelers were used to filter out mislabeled images. The author personally verified every label submitted by the labelers. Duplicate images were also removed after labeling.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The search term used to find an image provides a rough label, although it is described as extremely unreliable due to the nature of online image search technology. The tiny images dataset was assembled by searching for every non-abstract English noun in WordNet using web search engines and keeping roughly the first 3000 results for each term.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The tiny images dataset has no reliable class labels, making it hard to use for object recognition experiments. The rough labels from search terms are extremely unreliable. CIFAR-100 was only very recently completed at the time of writing, so experiments in the paper were only with CIFAR-10.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The tiny images dataset is described as an excellent dataset for unsupervised training of deep generative models. CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 were created for object recognition experiments. In the paper, CIFAR-10 is used for training and testing classifiers, with a training/test split where the training set receives 5000 randomly selected images from each class. CIFAR-100 classes are mutually exclusive with CIFAR-10 classes and can be used as negative examples for CIFAR-10.
